analysis.one_liner: Creates a government-run national health insurance program covering doctor, hospital, dental, and nursing care, funded by a new value-added tax.
analysis.headline: Dingell's national health insurance bill, introduced with zero cosponsors in the new Republican-led House, was referred to two health subcommittees, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have set up a national health insurance program run through a new National Health Insurance Board, with benefits administered by states and local areas. Workers and retirees who met wage or benefit thresholds — and their dependents — would be covered for physician, dental, hospital, home-nursing, and some auxiliary services, with free choice of doctor and hospital. Medicare beneficiaries would get coverage for services Medicare doesn't pay for. The program would be funded by a new value-added tax — a tax added at each stage of producing and selling goods and services — deposited into a dedicated National Health Care Trust Fund.
analysis.who_benefits: Working people whose wages qualify, retirees receiving Social Security or civil-service annuities, and their dependents gain guaranteed coverage with no premiums, deductibles, or network restrictions for covered services, plus free choice of physician and hospital. Needy individuals not otherwise eligible could be covered through payments by public agencies. Doctors, dentists, nurses, and hospitals that sign agreements keep their private practices and get guaranteed payment, though at regulated rates. Medicare recipients would gain coverage of gaps like deductibles and uncovered services.

how_it_helps.text: Every eligible individual gets medical, dental, podiatric, home-nursing, hospital (up to 60 days a year), and auxiliary services — including lab work, X-rays, prescribed expensive drugs, and eyeglasses — as benefits, choosing their own physician, dentist, and hospital.

There are no premiums or deductibles for covered services; eligibility rests on having earned modest wage thresholds in recent quarters, on receiving Social Security or civil-service retirement benefits, or on being a dependent of someone who qualifies.

Medicare beneficiaries can use the program for any services Medicare does not pay for, including deductible and coinsurance amounts, and a study was ordered on eventually folding Medicare into the new program.
Benefits cannot be denied on account of race, creed, or color, and the bill commits to decentralized, state-and-local administration with majority consumer representation on local committees.
Uninsured needy individuals can receive the same services through agreements with public agencies, funded partly by existing federal grants to states.

analysis.who_pays: Consumers and businesses would pay through a new value-added tax on taxable transactions, with the seller liable for the tax; retail food, housing, and medical care would be taxed at a zero rate. Private health insurers would lose their central role as payers, and employers' current role in arranging coverage would shrink. Doctors and hospitals would face regulated payment rates rather than market-negotiated charges.
analysis.who_pays_short: Consumers through the new sales tax

drawbacks.text: A value-added tax is a broad tax on consumption; even with food, housing, and medical care zero-rated, it still raises prices on most other goods and services, a burden that weighs relatively more on households that spend a large share of income.

Coverage is not universal: eligibility depends on meeting wage-history thresholds or receiving specific retirement benefits, and services for the non-eligible needy depend on public agencies agreeing to reimburse the fund.

Benefits can be limited: hospital coverage caps at 60 days a year (excludes most psychiatric hospitalization), and the Board may restrict dental, home-nursing, or auxiliary services whenever it finds personnel, facilities, or funds inadequate.
Providers would face Board-set payment rates and cost-based hospital reimbursement rather than negotiated charges, which hospitals and physician groups would lose negotiating leverage to resist.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered genuine, large benefits — guaranteed coverage without premiums or networks, free choice of doctor, and gap coverage for Medicare recipients — in exchange for a new broad-based tax whose burden would fall on consumers, and a less-than-universal eligibility structure with benefit limits. The trade-off was substantial and honestly framed in the bill's own findings, but the regressive tilt of a consumption tax and the limits on dental, nursing, and hospital coverage were real costs an honest supporter had to acknowledge. It was also a massive administrative undertaking layered on top of existing Medicare.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to two House committees and then to their health subcommittees, but no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Dingell introduced the National Health Insurance Act on January 4, 1995, the opening day of the 104th Congress, as the chamber shifted to Republican control.
No member joined as a cosponsor; the bill listed zero cosponsors for the entire Congress.

The Speaker referred it to both the Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee, and it was then sent to the Commerce health subcommittee in January and the Ways and Means Health and Environment Subcommittee in February 1995.
No further action was ever recorded — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill expired when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers kept their role as the payment system for health care, and businesses and consumers were spared the new value-added tax the bill would have imposed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private insurers; consumers spared the new tax

for.name: Rep. John D. Dingell
for.role: Sponsor, House Energy and Commerce Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the National Health Insurance Act on the first day of the 104th Congress and delivered introductory remarks on the floor.

against.name: Thomas J. Bliley Jr.
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill and referred it to the Health Subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing or markup for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Bill Archer
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill and referred it to the Health and Environment Subcommittee, where it sat without action for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held, so there is no roll-call record; the bill drew zero cosponsors from either party while a new Republican majority controlled both committees it was assigned to.

industries.note: The bill routes all payment for covered care through a public National Health Care Trust Fund, eliminating private insurers' core role as payer for medical, hospital, and dental services. Insurers' interest in stopping the bill ran against the bill's expansion of guaranteed coverage.

Providers who sign agreements get guaranteed payment from the trust fund and keep private practice, patient choice, and the right to reject patients, but payment rates are regulated and hospital payments are set on reasonable cost with Board-set maximums. The bill was deliberately structured to preserve private practice rather than employ doctors directly.

Hospitals would be paid reasonable costs for covered care — a guaranteed revenue stream — but under Board-prescribed maximum rates and least-expensive-accommodation rules, giving up pricing freedom. The bill bars federal supervision over hospital personnel and internal operations.

industries.industry: Businesses selling taxable goods and services
industries.note: Sellers become legally liable for remitting the new value-added tax, adding compliance costs, though the tax is generally passed to customers; food, housing, and medical care are exempted at a zero rate.
